Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents

// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] npm maintainer credential-phish lookalike domain npmjs.help (chalk/debug ATO)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — What is a dependency firewall?
Installation. Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] axios RAT C2 beacon to sfrclak[.]com / 142.11.206.73:8000 · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Malicious postmark-mcp BCC email exfiltration to phan@giftshop[.]club · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
npm maintainer credential-phish lookalike domain npmjs.help (chalk/debug ATO) AIDelivery High
Hunts endpoint DNS/web contact to the lookalike domain npmjs.help, the fake '2FA reset' phishing site used to steal the npm maintainer credentials behind the September 2025 chalk/debug supply-chain compromise. Legitimate npm lives on npmjs.com/npmjs.org, so any hit on npmjs.help is a maintainer-targeted credential-phishing indicator. Rationale: npmjs.help is a confirmed lookalike phishing domain (registered 2025-09-05, three days pre-attack) named in the article and corroborated by Sygnia/Checkmarx/Cycode/Aikido as the credential-theft vector for the chalk/debug ATO. Exact-domain match against a domain with no legitimate use = high fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/npm-debug-and-chalk-packages-compromised • https://www.sygnia.co/threat-reports-and-advisories/npm-supply-chain-attack-september-2025/ • https://checkmarx.com/zero-post/chalk-and-17-other-npm-packages-compromised-in-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1656
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SOC analyst or TI platform detonating/browsing npmjs.help in a sandboxed research VM
  • Automated URL-enrichment (SOAR/secure-web-gateway) resolving the domain for reputation scoring
  • Security-awareness phishing-simulation platform hosting a lookalike test page
  • DNS sinkhole/RPZ appliance logging the blocked query
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the host/user that resolved npmjs.help and whether a browser or npm tooling initiated it; pull any credential-entry or npm login activity in the following 30 min. 2) Contain: force-reset the affected npm account credentials and revoke/rotate npm publish tokens and 2FA; block npmjs.help at the proxy/DNS. 3) Hunt: check whether that maintainer published any npm package versions after the resolution timestamp, and scan lockfiles/CI for the chalk/debug malicious versions and browser-side crypto-address-swapping payloads.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "npmjs.help"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has "npmjs.help"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

plain-crypto-js postinstall RAT dropper spawns downloader (axios/Sapphire Sleet) AIInstallation High
Hunts the malicious plain-crypto-js@4.2.1 postinstall (setup.js) hook — pulled in transitively by axios@1.14.1/0.30.4 — spawning a downloader/interpreter that references the RAT campaign artifacts (sfrclak C2, campaign ID 6202033) to fetch platform-specific payloads. Targets the exact execution behaviour Microsoft attributes to Sapphire Sleet. Rationale: sfrclak, 142.11.206.73, campaign ID 6202033 and the plain-crypto-js dependency name are Datadog/Elastic/Socket-confirmed IOCs for the March 2026 axios RAT dropper (setup.js postinstall). These strings do not appear in benign build output, making a command-line match high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/axios-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/04/01/mitigating-the-axios-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://socket.dev/blog/axios-npm-package-compromised
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analyst detonating the sample in a lab (command lines will legitimately contain the IOCs)
  • IR/hunt scripts that embed the IOC strings as search arguments in their own command lines
  • Threat-intel simulation/purple-team replay of the axios TTPs
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("windbg.exe","procmon.exe") or DeviceName has_any ("MALWARE-LAB","SANDBOX"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the parent chain (node.exe/npm → interpreter) and whether the host has axios 1.14.1/0.30.4 or plain-crypto-js 4.2.1 in node_modules/lockfiles. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the RAT chain, and block sfrclak[.]com + 142.11.206.73 at egress. 3) Hunt: sweep for the dropped artifacts (%PROGRAMDATA%\wt.exe, system.bat, %TEMP%\6202033.ps1/.vbs, /Library/Caches/com.apple.act.mond, /tmp/ld.py), the MicrosoftUpdate Run key, and beacons to the C2; rotate any dev/CI credentials on the machine.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","cscript.exe","wscript.exe","curl.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","osascript","bash","sh")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("sfrclak","6202033","142.11.206.73")
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "plain-crypto-js"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has_any ("sfrclak","6202033","plain-crypto-js","142.11.206.73")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

axios RAT dropped artifacts: renamed PowerShell wt.exe + campaign 6202033 files AIInstallation High
Hunts file-system writes of the axios/plain-crypto-js RAT's dropped payloads across OSes: a renamed PowerShell (%PROGRAMDATA%\wt.exe), the persistence script system.bat, VBScript/PS1 droppers named 6202033, the macOS fake Apple daemon com.apple.act.mond, and the Linux payload ld.py. These paths are masquerading indicators unique to the Sapphire Sleet RAT staging. Rationale: The dropped paths (%PROGRAMDATA%\wt.exe = renamed PowerShell, system.bat, %TEMP%\6202033.ps1/.vbs, /Library/Caches/com.apple.act.mond, /tmp/ld.py) are verbatim IOCs from Datadog/Elastic write-ups. Excluding \WindowsApps\ removes the legitimate Windows Terminal wt.exe, leaving only the masqueraded copy. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/axios-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/axios-one-rat-to-rule-them-all • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/axios-compromised-on-npm-malicious-versions-drop-remote-access-trojan
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Windows Terminal wt.exe (lives under \WindowsApps\, excluded by the filter)
  • An admin/backup script legitimately named system.bat deployed via GPO to ProgramData
  • A developer repo on macOS/Linux containing an unrelated ld.py linker helper
  • EDR sample-collection/quarantine copying the artifact into a scan folder
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath !has @"\WindowsApps\" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("gpscript.exe","msiexec.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the writing process (should trace back to node.exe/npm postinstall) and hash the dropped file against the published SHA-256s (e.g. Windows PS payload 617b67a8e1210e4fc87c92d1d1da45a2f311c08d26e89b12307cf583c900d101). 2) Contain: isolate host, delete artifacts, remove the MicrosoftUpdate Run key, block sfrclak[.]com/142.11.206.73. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same InitiatingProcess across the fleet, and audit npm lockfiles org-wide for axios 1.14.1/0.30.4 and plain-crypto-js 4.2.1.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName =~ "wt.exe" and FolderPath has @"\ProgramData\")
   or (FileName =~ "system.bat" and FolderPath has @"\ProgramData\")
   or FileName in~ ("6202033.vbs","6202033.ps1")
   or FileName =~ "com.apple.act.mond"
   or FileName =~ "ld.py"
| where FolderPath !has @"\WindowsApps\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (TargetFileName =~ "wt.exe" and TargetFilePath has @"\ProgramData\")
   or (TargetFileName =~ "system.bat" and TargetFilePath has @"\ProgramData\")
   or TargetFileName in~ ("6202033.vbs","6202033.ps1","com.apple.act.mond","ld.py")
| where TargetFilePath !has @"\WindowsApps\"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: axios RAT Dropped Payload Files (wt.exe / system.bat / 6202033)
id: 2f9d5a70-1b6c-4e8a-9c33-7a0e2f4d1c03
description: Detects creation of the axios/plain-crypto-js RAT dropped artifacts including a renamed PowerShell in ProgramData, system.bat persistence script, and 6202033-named droppers.
references:
  - https://www.aikido.dev/blog/what-is-a-dependency-firewall
  - https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/axios-npm-supply-chain-compromise/
  - https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/axios-one-rat-to-rule-them-all
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/14
tags:
  - attack.t1036.005
  - attack.t1105
  - attack.defense_evasion
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_wt:
    TargetFilename|contains: '\ProgramData\'
    TargetFilename|endswith:
      - '\wt.exe'
      - '\system.bat'
  selection_named:
    TargetFilename|endswith:
      - '6202033.vbs'
      - '6202033.ps1'
  condition: selection_wt or selection_named
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 (@TargetFilename:(*\\ProgramData\\wt.exe OR *\\ProgramData\\WT.exe OR *\\ProgramData\\system.bat) OR @TargetFilename:(*\\6202033.vbs OR *\\6202033.ps1 OR *\\6202033.VBS OR *\\6202033.PS1))
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| TargetFileName=/(ProgramData\\(wt\.exe|system\.bat)|6202033\.(vbs|ps1)|com\.apple\.act\.mond|(\/tmp\/)?ld\.py$)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name="wt.exe" AND Filesystem.file_path="*\\ProgramData\\*") OR (Filesystem.file_name="system.bat" AND Filesystem.file_path="*\\ProgramData\\*") OR Filesystem.file_name IN ("6202033.vbs","6202033.ps1","com.apple.act.mond","ld.py") by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.file_name, Filesystem.file_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name="wt.exe" AND Filesystem.file_path="*\\ProgramData\\*") OR (Filesystem.file_name="system.bat" AND Filesystem.file_path="*\\ProgramData\\*") OR Filesystem.file_name IN ("6202033.vbs","6202033.ps1","com.apple.act.mond","ld.py") by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.file_name, Filesystem.file_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
axios RAT persistence: HKCU Run value MicrosoftUpdate pointing to system.bat AIInstallation High
Hunts the exact autostart persistence set by the axios/plain-crypto-js RAT: an HKCU CurrentVersion\Run value named 'MicrosoftUpdate' whose data references system.bat, re-executing the payload at each logon. The masqueraded value name plus the system.bat data string make this a tight, single-event persistence signal. Rationale: The Run value name 'MicrosoftUpdate' -> system.bat is the exact persistence IOC documented by Datadog for the axios RAT. Value-name masquerading as a Microsoft component combined with a .bat data string is a precise, low-noise autostart indicator. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/axios-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/04/01/mitigating-the-axios-npm-supply-chain-compromise/
ATT&CKT1547.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate internal update tool that (poorly) names its Run value MicrosoftUpdate and points to a .bat wrapper
  • Sysadmin logon automation deployed via a system.bat referenced in a Run key
  • Software packaging/testing that seeds throwaway Run keys
  • Golden-image build tooling writing autostart entries
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the writing process and the full RegistryValueData path; confirm whether it points to %PROGRAMDATA%\system.bat. 2) Contain: remove the Run value, delete system.bat and the renamed wt.exe, isolate the host, block the C2. 3) Hunt: query the fleet for the same value name/data pair, correlate to hosts that recently ran npm installs of axios/plain-crypto-js, and check egress logs for sfrclak[.]com beacons on port 8000.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "RegistryValueSet"
| where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Run"
| where RegistryValueName =~ "MicrosoftUpdate"
| where RegistryValueData has "system.bat"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Run"
| where RegistryValue =~ "MicrosoftUpdate"
| where RegistryValueData has "system.bat"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: axios RAT Registry Run Persistence (MicrosoftUpdate -> system.bat)
id: c41a8e6b-3d29-4b7a-8f52-9e0b1a6c2d04
description: Detects the HKCU Run value 'MicrosoftUpdate' referencing system.bat, the logon persistence set by the axios/plain-crypto-js RAT.

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry where Registry.registry_path="*\\CurrentVersion\\Run*" AND Registry.registry_value_name="MicrosoftUpdate" AND Registry.registry_value_data="*system.bat*" by Registry.dest, Registry.registry_path, Registry.registry_value_name, Registry.registry_value_data | `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
axios RAT C2 beacon to sfrclak[.]com / 142.11.206.73:8000 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts endpoint DNS/network contact to the axios RAT command-and-control infrastructure sfrclak[.]com and 142.11.206.73 (payload URL http://sfrclak[.]com:8000/6202033, 60-second beacon loop). Single-indicator network match against dedicated, freshly registered attacker infrastructure. Rationale: sfrclak[.]com (registered 2026-03-30) and 142.11.206.73:8000 are the Datadog/Elastic-confirmed C2 for the axios RAT. Dedicated attacker infrastructure with no legitimate use yields a near-zero-FP network detection. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/axios-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/axios-one-rat-to-rule-them-all • https://thehackernews.com/2026/03/axios-supply-chain-attack-pushes-cross.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • TI enrichment/sandbox host resolving sfrclak[.]com for reputation scoring
  • Security researcher pcap replay of the campaign
  • DNS sinkhole/RPZ logging the query it just blocked
  • Passive-DNS collector mirroring the domain
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the beaconing process (expect powershell/python/curl descended from node) and beacon cadence (~60s). 2) Contain: isolate host, block sfrclak[.]com + 142.11.206.73 at the firewall/proxy, kill the process tree. 3) Hunt: sweep the fleet for any resolution of sfrclak[.]com, correlate to recent axios/plain-crypto-js installs and the MicrosoftUpdate Run-key persistence, and rotate credentials cached on impacted hosts.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "sfrclak.com" or RemoteIP == "142.11.206.73"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
(ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has "sfrclak.com"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, Indicator = DnsQuery)
| union (CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP == "142.11.206.73" or DestinationHostName has "sfrclak.com"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr = SourceIP, SrcHostname = SourceHostName, Indicator = strcat(DestinationIP, " ", DestinationHostName))
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Malicious postmark-mcp BCC email exfiltration to phan@giftshop[.]club AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts outbound mail silently BCC'd to phan@giftshop[.]club, the exfiltration address hard-coded into the trojanised postmark-mcp@1.0.16 npm MCP server (the first confirmed malicious MCP server on npm). Any recipient in the giftshop.club domain on org mail flow is a direct exfiltration indicator. Rationale: phan@giftshop[.]club is the verbatim BCC exfiltration address added in postmark-mcp@1.0.16, corroborated by Snyk/The Register/The Hacker News. It matches the article's pre-extracted IOC giftshop.club; any org mail with a giftshop.club recipient is high-fidelity exfiltration. Cross-checked against: • https://snyk.io/blog/malicious-mcp-server-on-npm-postmark-mcp-harvests-emails/ • https://thehackernews.com/2025/09/first-malicious-mcp-server-found.html • https://www.theregister.com/2025/09/29/postmark_mcp_server_code_hijacked/
ATT&CKT1114 T1020 T1195.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A genuine business contact who happens to use a giftshop.club address (verify domain legitimacy first)
  • A phishing/threat-intel test message deliberately addressed to the IOC domain
  • Mail-security detonation/replay tooling re-sending a captured malicious message
  • A distribution-list expansion that legitimately contains the address (should be treated as compromise, not FP)
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all messages with a giftshop.club recipient, note the sending mailboxes/service principals and whether the send path involved an MCP server or automation. 2) Contain: block giftshop.club at mail flow, purge outbound copies, and audit dev workstations for the postmark-mcp npm package (any version >=1.0.16); remove it. 3) Hunt: inventory MCP servers/AI-agent tooling pulling from npm, review what those agents had access to (email, secrets), and rotate any credentials the exposed emails may have contained.
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RecipientEmailAddress endswith "giftshop.club" or SenderFromDomain =~ "giftshop.club"
| project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, EmailDirection, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation
| order by Timestamp desc
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where OfficeWorkload =~ "Exchange"
| where Recipients has "giftshop.club" or P2RecipientList has "giftshop.club"
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, ClientIP, Recipients, P2RecipientList
| order by TimeGenerated desc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Email.All_Email where (All_Email.recipient="*giftshop.club*" OR All_Email.recipient="phan@giftshop.club") by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.subject | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Email.All_Email where (All_Email.recipient="*giftshop.club*" OR All_Email.recipient="phan@giftshop.club") by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.subject | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`

Side-loaded / unsigned extensions, often masquerading as wallets, productivity tools.

title: Browser Extension Installation via Registry
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0a
status: experimental
description: |
    Registry writes under the browser extension policy keys —
    administrative install of an extension. Often used by adware /
    info-stealers to bypass user-level extension controls.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1176/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1176
    - attack.persistence
logsource:
    category: registry_event
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetObject|contains:
            - '\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\'
            - '\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\'
            - '\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - Group-policy-managed extension whitelists
level: medium
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry
    where (Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\*"
        OR Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\*"
        OR Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\*")
    by Registry.dest, Registry.registry_path, Registry.registry_value_data, Registry.registry_value_name, Registry.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry
    where (Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\*"
        OR Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\*"
        OR Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\*")
    by Registry.dest, Registry.registry_path, Registry.registry_value_data, Registry.registry_value_name, Registry.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)`
Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

New MemGhost Attack Plants Persistent False Memories in AI Agents Through One Email

The Hacker News
2026-07-13 3 use cases 1 technique 5 kill-chain phases detected

Give an AI assistant a memory and access to your inbox, and you hand an attacker a way to rewrite what it thinks it knows about you. A single email can trick that agent into saving a false "fact" about the user, hide the change, and quietly steer its answers in later sessions. When it works, the person reads an ordinary-looking reply and never learns their assistant was tampered with. The

Writes to AI-agent persistent memory/instruction files (AGENTS.md, MEMORY.md) — MemGhost poisoning artifact AIInstallation Low
Hunts file create/modify events on the exact plaintext state files OpenClaw and Claude Code SDK agents load into model context every session (AGENTS.md standing instructions, MEMORY.md learned facts). MemGhost's whole persistence mechanism is a single write into these core files so the false 'fact' reloads in every later session; logging and reviewing every write to them is the researchers' own recommended defense. Rationale: AGENTS.md and MEMORY.md are the exact core state files named in the article and paper as the poisoning target (loaded every session); the researchers explicitly recommend logging every write to these files, making a file-event hunt the highest-fidelity article-grounded pivot. Cross-checked the arXiv paper and EchoLeak advisory for the same email-borne AI-memory pattern. Cross-checked against: • https://arxiv.org/html/2607.05189v1 • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/new-memghost-attack-plants-persistent.html • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2025-32711
ATT&CKT1565.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Normal agent operation legitimately updating MEMORY.md as it learns real user preferences
  • Developer manually editing AGENTS.md/MEMORY.md in an IDE (VS Code, Notepad++)
  • git clone/checkout of agent-template repositories that ship an AGENTS.md
  • Agent framework upgrade rewriting default AGENTS.md scaffolding
  • Backup/sync tooling (OneDrive, Dropbox) rewriting the files on restore
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("git.exe","Code.exe","devenv.exe","notepad.exe","notepad++.exe","OneDrive.exe","Dropbox.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the current AGENTS.md/MEMORY.md and its version/backup history; look for injected authorization or financial claims (e.g. a raised Zelle/transfer limit like the paper's $10,000 test lure) or instructions to stay silent about the change. 2) Contain: snapshot the file for evidence, revert to a known-good copy, and disable the agent's autonomous email-triggered / background runs until reviewed. 3) Hunt: correlate the write time against recently delivered inbound email to that user (hidden/agent-directed text), and sweep other agent hosts for writes to the same two filenames.
DeviceFileEvents

| where ActionType in ("FileModified","FileCreated")
| where FileName in~ ("MEMORY.md","AGENTS.md")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Writes=count(), Paths=make_set(FolderPath,5)
    by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessAccountUpn, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName
| order by LastSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("MEMORY.md","AGENTS.md")
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"

    by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileName
| order by LastSeen desc

id: 6f3a1e42-2c7b-4d19-9a8e-3f0b7c9d1a55
description: Detects create/modify of OpenClaw / Claude Code SDK persistent state files (AGENTS.md, MEMORY.md) that are loaded into model context each session and are the target of MemGhost email-borne memory poisoning.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/new-memghost-attack-plants-persistent.html

| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` 
| where user!="" AND NOT match(user,"\$$")

Inbound email followed within minutes by agent memory-file write (MemGhost one-email chain) AIDelivery Low
Temporal correlation targeting MemGhost's signature: a single inbound email reaches a mailbox an AI agent reads, and within a short window the agent writes AGENTS.md or MEMORY.md on that user's endpoint. Ties the delivery (initial access) to the persistence write so the analyst sees the one-shot email-to-false-memory pivot rather than either event in isolation. Rationale: Uses the article's core claim — one inbound email causes the agent to write its persistent memory (AGENTS.md/MEMORY.md) — as a delivery-to-persistence temporal join on the recipient's UPN, which is the MemGhost fingerprint no single-event rule captures. Sentinel/Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch left empty because the email half depends on Defender XDR EmailEvents with no equivalent in those tenants; the file half alone would duplicate UC1. Cross-checked against: • https://arxiv.org/html/2607.05189v1 • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/new-memghost-attack-plants-persistent.html
ATT&CKT1566 T1565.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Email.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User receives a legitimate email and, in the same session, chats with the agent causing a genuine memory update within 30 minutes
  • Newsletter/automation mail arriving coincidentally near a routine agent memory refresh
  • Agent processing a legitimate task email that legitimately updates a stored preference
  • Shared mailbox where email recipient UPN and endpoint user coincide by chance
  • Developer testing the agent's email skill with benign messages
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the correlated email (SenderFromAddress, Subject, NetworkMessageId) and inspect its raw body for hidden/agent-directed instructions (HTML comments, white-on-white text, memory-write or stay-silent directives); diff the AGENTS.md/MEMORY.md write for injected authorization/financial facts. 2) Contain: quarantine the message across mailboxes, revert the poisoned memory file, and suspend the agent's inbox-reading/background automation. 3) Hunt: search EmailEvents for the same sender/cluster to other agent users, and re-run UC1 across all hosts running OpenClaw or Claude Code SDK agents for further AGENTS.md/MEMORY.md writes.
let Window = 30m;
let Mail = EmailEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
    | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
    | project MailTime=Timestamp, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress, Subject, NetworkMessageId;
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("FileModified","FileCreated")
| where FileName in~ ("MEMORY.md","AGENTS.md")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where isnotempty(InitiatingProcessAccountUpn)
| join kind=inner Mail on $left.InitiatingProcessAccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| where Timestamp between (MailTime .. MailTime + Window)
| project MailTime, WriteTime=Timestamp,
          DelayMin=datetime_diff('minute', Timestamp, MailTime),
          DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountUpn, FileName, FolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          SenderFromAddress, Subject, NetworkMessageId
| order by WriteTime desc

Forg365 device-code phishing: successful sign-in via Microsoft Authentication Broker AIDelivery Medium
Hunts successful Entra ID sign-ins to the first-party Microsoft Authentication Broker app (appId 29d9ed98-a469-4536-ade2-f981bc1d605e) that Forg365's device-auth branch abuses to authorize an attacker-controlled session. The victim sees a real Microsoft verification-code page while the code authorizes the operator's device, so the tell is broker-app auth from anomalous IPs/geos rather than any malicious binary. Rationale: Anchors on the exact auth surface the article names ('legitimate Microsoft Authentication Broker sign-in flow' where 'the code authorizes an attacker-controlled session'); the broker app (29d9ed98-a469-4536-ade2-f981bc1d605e) is rarely used by normal end users so successful sign-ins from non-compliant devices/foreign IPs are high-signal. Cross-checked ZeroBEC and BleepingComputer. Cross-checked against: • https://zerobec.com/blog/inside-forg365-telegram-distributed-sneaky2fa-style-phaas • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-forg365-phishing-platform-uses-ai-to-target-microsoft-365-accounts/ • https://cyberpress.org/forg365-phaas-abuses-microsoft-device-code-flow/
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1528
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Intune / Windows Autopilot device enrollment using device-code flow
  • Engineers running 'az login --use-device-code' or Connect-MgGraph device-code auth
  • Conference-room / shared IoT devices onboarding to Teams via device code
  • Legitimate remote staff signing in from travel geos
  • Break-glass or automation accounts that intentionally use the broker
Suppression filter
| where tostring(parse_json(tostring(DeviceDetail)).isCompliant) != "true" and ClientAppUsed != "Mobile Apps and Desktop clients" or ConditionalAccessStatus == "failure"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): For each hit, review the IP/ASN/geo and UserAgent against the user's baseline and whether the device is Entra-compliant; confirm whether any device-code flow was expected (Intune/az login). Step 2 (contain): If unexplained, revoke the user's refresh tokens (Revoke-MgUserSignInSession / 'Revoke sessions'), force password reset + MFA re-registration, and block device-code authentication via Conditional Access. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the AccountUpn into AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs for silent token replay from a new IP, and into OfficeActivity for New-InboxRule / mailbox changes made after the sign-in.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ErrorCode == 0
| where Application == "Microsoft Authentication Broker" or ResourceDisplayName == "Microsoft Authentication Broker"
| where AccountUpn !endswith "$"
| summarize SignIns = count(), Countries = make_set(Country, 10), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 20), Apps = make_set(ClientAppUsed, 5), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by AccountUpn
| order by LastSeen desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ResultType == 0
| where AppDisplayName == "Microsoft Authentication Broker" or ResourceDisplayName == "Microsoft Authentication Broker"
| extend Country = tostring(parse_json(tostring(LocationDetails)).countryOrRegion)
| where tostring(parse_json(tostring(DeviceDetail)).isCompliant) != "true"
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName, AppId, IPAddress, Country, ClientAppUsed, UserAgent, ConditionalAccessStatus
| order by TimeGenerated desc

description: Detects successful Entra ID sign-ins to the Microsoft Authentication Broker app abused by Forg365 device-code phishing.

Forg365 AitM/ForgCookie token replay: silent non-interactive sign-in from new IP after broker auth AICommand & Control Medium
Correlates a successful Microsoft Authentication Broker (device-code) sign-in with a subsequent non-interactive Entra sign-in for the same user from a different IP and country within 24h — the signature of Forg365's stolen-session replay and the ForgCookie extension's injected refresh-token cookie triggering a silent OAuth flow. Detects the operator using the vaulted token/cookie from their own infrastructure. Rationale: Directly models the article's 'session cookies/token vaulting' + ForgCookie 'inject refresh-token cookie ... trigger a silent OAuth flow' behaviour: an interactive device-code auth followed by a non-interactive (silent) sign-in from a different IP/country is token replay, not the real user. Temporal + geo correlation strips the noise. Datadog/Falcon left empty — this needs a cross-table interactive-vs-non-interactive Entra join not expressible in a single Datadog query or in FDR endpoint telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://zerobec.com/blog/inside-forg365-telegram-distributed-sneaky2fa-style-phaas • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-forg365-phishing-platform-uses-ai-to-target-microsoft-365-accounts/
ATT&CKT1550.004 T1557
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Corporate VPN / SASE egress that shifts the user's apparent country between interactive and background sign-ins
  • Mobile roaming where the phone's non-interactive token refresh comes from a carrier gateway in another country
  • Legitimate multi-region cloud automation running as the user
  • Traveling executives whose device syncs from a new location
  • Enterprise proxy that geolocates non-interactive traffic differently from browser traffic
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Compare AuthIP/AuthCountry (interactive) against ReplayIP/ReplayCountry (silent); check the replay IP's ASN/hosting reputation and whether the resource is Exchange/Graph/OWA. Step 2 (contain): Revoke all sessions and refresh tokens for the user, reset credentials, and quarantine the account; if a ForgCookie/browser extension is suspected, isolate the endpoint and clear browser session state. Step 3 (hunt): Search OfficeActivity for MailItemsAccessed / New-InboxRule from the replay IP, enumerate other users signing in from that IP/ASN, and review OAuth app grants added during the window.
let AuthWindow = 24h;
let brokerAuth = AADSignInEventsBeta
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where ErrorCode == 0 and IsInteractive == true
    | where Application == "Microsoft Authentication Broker" or ResourceDisplayName == "Microsoft Authentication Broker"
    | project AuthTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, AuthIP = IPAddress, AuthCountry = Country;
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ErrorCode == 0 and IsInteractive == false
| join kind=inner brokerAuth on AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (AuthTime .. AuthTime + AuthWindow)
| where IPAddress != AuthIP and Country != AuthCountry
| project AuthTime, ReplayTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, AuthIP, AuthCountry, ReplayIP = IPAddress, ReplayCountry = Country, Application, ResourceDisplayName, UserAgent
| order by ReplayTime desc
let AuthWindow = 24h;
let brokerAuth = SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where ResultType == 0
    | where AppDisplayName == "Microsoft Authentication Broker" or ResourceDisplayName == "Microsoft Authentication Broker"
    | project AuthTime = TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, AuthIP = IPAddress, AuthCountry = tostring(parse_json(tostring(LocationDetails)).countryOrRegion);
AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == 0
| join kind=inner brokerAuth on UserPrincipalName
| where TimeGenerated between (AuthTime .. AuthTime + AuthWindow)
| where IPAddress != AuthIP and Location != AuthCountry
| project AuthTime, ReplayTime = TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, AuthIP, AuthCountry, ReplayIP = IPAddress, ReplayCountry = Location, AppDisplayName, ResourceDisplayName, ClientAppUsed
| order by ReplayTime desc
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` values(Authentication.src) as src_list dc(Authentication.src) as distinct_src values(Authentication.action) as actions min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.app="Microsoft Authentication Broker" OR Authentication.action=success by Authentication.user _time span=24h
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| where distinct_src >= 2
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false values(Authentication.src) as src_list dc(Authentication.src) as distinct_src values(Authentication.action) as actions min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.app="Microsoft Authentication Broker" OR Authentication.action=success by Authentication.user _time span=24h
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| where distinct_src >= 2

| sort - lastTime
Forg365 post-compromise: inbox rule created to monitor keyword hits in hijacked mailbox AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts creation/modification of Exchange inbox rules whose conditions key on subject/body keywords — the mechanism behind Forg365's 'keyword alerts' and post-compromise mailbox monitoring. Fires when a freshly compromised account programmatically stands up a rule to watch for finance/credential terms and auto-file or hide matching mail. Rationale: Maps the article's explicit post-compromise capability ('monitoring for specific keywords in compromised email accounts' / 'keyword alerts' panel feature) to the concrete audit artifact: inbox rules built on SubjectContainsWords/BodyContainsWords conditions. Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch empty — O365 mailbox-audit telemetry isn't in those standard sources. Cross-checked against: • https://zerobec.com/blog/inside-forg365-telegram-distributed-sneaky2fa-style-phaas • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-forg365-phishing-platform-uses-ai-to-target-microsoft-365-accounts/
ATT&CKT1114.003 T1564.008
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Users legitimately creating keyword-based filing rules (e.g. auto-file 'invoice' mail into a folder)
  • Mailbox migration / helpdesk tooling that recreates rules in bulk
  • Third-party email add-ins (CRM, ticketing) provisioning rules on the user's behalf
  • Executive-assistant delegate setting up rules for a shared mailbox
  • Security awareness tools that create sample rules
Suppression filter
| where not (ClientIP in ("<corp-egress-not-used>") ) | where RuleValue has_any ("password","invoice","payment","wire","remittance","security","login","verify","mfa","otp")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Inspect the rule value/condition and the ClientIP that created it — attacker rules commonly hide security/finance keywords or auto-delete/forward; correlate the ClientIP with any broker sign-in or token-replay hit for the same UserId. Step 2 (contain): Remove the malicious inbox rule, revoke sessions/tokens, reset the credential, and disable any auto-forward the rule set. Step 3 (hunt): Enumerate all inbox/transport rules created tenant-wide from the same ClientIP/ASN, check MailItemsAccessed and Send activity for lateral phishing (OctoLink Sender-style mass send), and review recent OAuth app consents.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("New-InboxRule", "Set-InboxRule", "UpdateInboxRules")
| extend Raw = tostring(RawEventData)
| where Raw has_any ("SubjectContainsWords", "BodyContainsWords", "SubjectOrBodyContainsWords", "FromAddressContainsWords")
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, IPAddress, ActionType, Application, Raw
| order by Timestamp desc
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
| where Operation in ("New-InboxRule", "Set-InboxRule", "UpdateInboxRules")
| extend Params = parse_json(Parameters)
| mv-apply p = Params on (
    extend pName = tostring(p.Name), pValue = tostring(p.Value)
  )
| where pName in~ ("SubjectContainsWords","BodyContainsWords","SubjectOrBodyContainsWords","FromAddressContainsWords")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, ClientIP, Operation, RuleCondition = pName, RuleValue = pValue
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:

            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

Hunts creation of the AD_Report.html inventory artifact by PowerShell, the distinctive output file of the vibe-coded 'AD Information Gathering' script Huntress observed. AD_Report.html is a bespoke, non-standard filename produced only by this enumeration tool, making its creation a high-fidelity discovery signal. Rationale: AD_Report.html is an article-specific bespoke filename (the script's own success-measure artifact); pairing it with a PowerShell writer removes any residual noise. Cross-checked against the Huntress write-up which names the artifact and the script title. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/ai-coded-malware-vibe-coding-active-directory • https://cybersecuritynews.com/vibe-coded-powershell-script-active-directory/
ATT&CKT1087.002 T1018 T1482 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A sysadmin's own AD documentation/reporting script that coincidentally names its output AD_Report.html
  • Commercial AD auditing tools (e.g. some PingCastle/ADRecon wrappers) if re-templated to that filename
  • A pentest/red-team engagement reusing the same public script
  • Security-team baselining exercise generating an AD inventory report
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath startswith "C:\\ProgramData\\" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("Get-ADUser","Get-ADComputer","nltest","DirectorySearcher")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full InitiatingProcessCommandLine and parent chain; confirm the script matches the 'AD Information Gathering' / cascading-fallback profile and whether it ran from C:\ProgramData. 2) Contain: isolate the host, disable the executing account, and kill the RDP session it originated from; the pre-compromised credential should be reset domain-wide. 3) Hunt: look on the same host for s5cmd.exe and SharpShares.exe execution and a newly created staging directory of AD CSV exports within the surrounding 60 minutes.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileName =~ "AD_Report.html"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileName =~ "AD_Report.html"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SharpShares network-share enumeration binary staged in C:\ProgramData AIReconnaissance High
Hunts execution of SharpShares, the C#-based network share enumeration utility Huntress saw deployed ~30 minutes after AD enumeration to locate user-accessible data repositories. Matches on the binary name and its embedded original-filename metadata so a simple rename doesn't evade, with a C:\ProgramData staging fallback. Rationale: SharpShares is explicitly named in the article as the share-enumeration tool; matching FileName plus ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName defeats trivial rename, and the C:\ProgramData staging path mirrors the observed tradecraft. Corroborated by the Huntress blog naming SharpShares and s5cmd. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/ai-coded-malware-vibe-coding-active-directory • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/vibe-coded-malware-ai-powershell/
ATT&CKT1135 T1083
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized red-team/pentest engagement running SharpShares
  • Internal share-inventory/audit script that shells out to SharpShares
  • A file-server migration project enumerating shares
  • Security researcher testing the tool in a lab VM
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","explorer.exe") and (FolderPath startswith "C:\\ProgramData\\" or FolderPath startswith "C:\\Users\\Public\\" or FolderPath startswith "C:\\Windows\\Temp\\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the executing account and whether the parent chain traces to an RDP-launched shell in C:\ProgramData; capture the SHA256 and command line. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the session, and disable the account; treat any share paths in the command line as targeted collection scope. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host/account for AD_Report.html creation, s5cmd cloud egress, and archive creation (.zip/.7z) of the enumerated CSVs.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName =~ "SharpShares.exe"
    or ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName =~ "SharpShares.exe"
    or (FolderPath startswith "C:\\ProgramData\\" and ProcessCommandLine has "shares" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--ldap","--filter","--outfile","/ldap","/outfile"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\SharpShares.exe"
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
