title: Outbound Connection to Article-Named IP / Domain
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0f
status: experimental
description: |
    Replace `__IP_LIST__` / `__DOMAIN_LIST__` placeholders with
    article-specific destinations. For dynamic IOC management, use a
    watchlist or external feed.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0011/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.command-and-control
logsource:
    category: network_connection
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_ip:
        DestinationIp:
            - '__IP_PLACEHOLDER_1__'
            - '__IP_PLACEHOLDER_2__'
    selection_domain:
        DestinationHostname:
            - '__DOMAIN_PLACEHOLDER_1__'
            - '__DOMAIN_PLACEHOLDER_2__'
    condition: selection_ip or selection_domain
falsepositives:
    - None on a true-positive IOC match
level: critical
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.dest IN ("37.27.122.124", "57.128.246.79")
    by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest, All_Traffic.dest_port
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| append
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Web
        where Web.dest IN ("")
        by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.url, Web.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`]
| append
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS
        where DNS.query IN ("")
        by DNS.src, DNS.query, DNS.answer
     | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`]
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.dest IN ("37.27.122.124", "57.128.246.79")
    by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest, All_Traffic.dest_port
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| append
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web
        where Web.dest IN ("")
        by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.url, Web.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`]
| append
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS
        where DNS.query IN ("")
        by DNS.src, DNS.query, DNS.answer
     | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`]
Suspicious browser extension installation Installation Medium
Side-loaded / unsigned extensions, often masquerading as wallets, productivity tools.
ATT&CKT1176
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry DeviceRegistryEvents
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where RegistryKey has_any ("\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\","\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\","\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where RegistryKey has_any (@"\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\",
                              @"\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\",
                              @"\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, RegistryKey,
          RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Browser Extension Installation via Registry
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0a
status: experimental
description: |
    Registry writes under the browser extension policy keys —
    administrative install of an extension. Often used by adware /
    info-stealers to bypass user-level extension controls.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1176/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1176
    - attack.persistence
logsource:
    category: registry_event
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetObject|contains:
            - '\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\'
            - '\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\'
            - '\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - Group-policy-managed extension whitelists
level: medium
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry
    where (Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\*"
        OR Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\*"
        OR Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\*")
    by Registry.dest, Registry.registry_path, Registry.registry_value_data, Registry.registry_value_name, Registry.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry
    where (Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\*"
        OR Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\*"
        OR Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\*")
    by Registry.dest, Registry.registry_path, Registry.registry_value_data, Registry.registry_value_name, Registry.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)`
Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process Actions on Objectives High
Stealers / wallet drainers read keystore.json, MetaMask, Exodus, Atomic, Phantom data.
ATT&CKT1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Ethereum\keystore\", @"\Bitcoin\", @"\Exodus\", @"\Electrum\wallets\", @"\MetaMask\", @"\Phantom\", @"\Atomic\Local Storage\")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MetaMask.exe","Exodus.exe","Atomic.exe","electrum.exe","Bitcoin.exe","Phantom.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Ethereum\keystore\", @"\Bitcoin\",
                                  @"\Exodus\", @"\Electrum\wallets\",
                                  @"\MetaMask\", @"\Phantom\",
                                  @"\Atomic\Local Storage\")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("MetaMask.exe","Exodus.exe","Atomic.exe",
                                  "electrum.exe","Bitcoin.exe","Phantom.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Crypto-Wallet Keystore Access by Non-Wallet Process
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d02
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers / wallet drainers read keystore files from MetaMask,
    Exodus, Atomic, Phantom, Bitcoin, Electrum, Ethereum-cli wallets.
    Filtering out the legitimate wallet binaries leaves only attacker
    activity.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1005/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1005
    - attack.collection
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Ethereum\keystore\'
            - '\Bitcoin\'
            - '\Exodus\'
            - '\Electrum\wallets\'
            - '\MetaMask\'
            - '\Phantom\'
            - '\Atomic\Local Storage\'
    filter_legit:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\MetaMask.exe'
            - '\Exodus.exe'
            - '\Atomic.exe'
            - '\electrum.exe'
            - '\Bitcoin.exe'
            - '\Phantom.exe'
    condition: selection_path and not filter_legit
falsepositives:
    - Backup software
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Ethereum\keystore\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Bitcoin\wallet.dat"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Exodus\exodus.wallet*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Electrum\wallets\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\MetaMask\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Phantom\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Atomic\Local Storage\*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("MetaMask.exe","Exodus.exe","Atomic.exe","electrum.exe","Bitcoin.exe","Phantom.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Ethereum\keystore\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Bitcoin\wallet.dat"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Exodus\exodus.wallet*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Electrum\wallets\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\MetaMask\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Phantom\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Atomic\Local Storage\*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("MetaMask.exe","Exodus.exe","Atomic.exe","electrum.exe","Bitcoin.exe","Phantom.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command Exploitation High
Encoded or obfuscated PowerShell — common across loaders, recon, and post-exploitation.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.execution
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for
      cross-shell escaping
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd") or SHA1 in~ ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd") or MD5 in~ ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd") or SHA1 in~ ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd") or MD5 in~ ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Compromised jscrambler 8.14.0 npm Release Drops Rust Infostealer During Install

The Hacker News
2026-07-11 14 use cases 5 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

The jscrambler npm package was compromised, and simply installing its&nbsp;8.14.0&nbsp;release runs an infostealer on your machine. Published on July 11, 2026, the malicious version carries a&nbsp;preinstall&nbsp;hook that drops and executes a native binary, one build each for Windows, macOS, and Linux. jscrambler 8.14.0 npm Package Installation AIDelivery High
Hunts for installation of the compromised jscrambler CLI npm package (8.14.0 and the sibling malicious versions 8.16.0/8.17.0/8.18.0/8.20.0 tied to the same actor) via npm/pnpm/yarn command lines on developer and CI hosts. Article-specific because it pins the exact package name and poisoned version window rather than generic npm abuse. Rationale: Anchors on the exact package name 'jscrambler' plus the poisoned version set from the article (8.14.0) enriched with the sibling malicious versions Socket attributed to the same actor. Version-pinned package name in an install command is very high fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/jscrambler-supply-chain-attack • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-backdoor-jscrambler-npm-package-with-infostealer-malware/
ATT&CKT1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A dependency-audit or SCA tool that echoes 'jscrambler@8.14.0' in its scan output command line
  • A remediation script explicitly uninstalling/overriding jscrambler@8.14.0 (npm uninstall / npm ls output)
  • A CI lockfile-pinning job that references the version string while forcing an upgrade to 8.15.0
  • A developer reproducing the incident in an isolated sandbox
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("uninstall","npm ls","npm audit","remove"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the command was an install (npm install/ci/add) not an uninstall/audit, and check whether the host is a build agent or developer laptop with access to cloud keys. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill any node.exe child processes, and remove jscrambler@8.14.0 from lockfiles/caches; pin to 8.13.0 or 8.15.0. 3) Hunt: on any confirmed install, treat all reachable secrets as stolen — rotate AWS/Azure/GCP keys, npm/GitHub tokens, and AI-tool/MCP API keys; pivot to UC2/UC3 to find the dropped binary and C2 callbacks.

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","pnpm.exe","yarn.exe") or FileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "jscrambler" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("8.14.0","8.16.0","8.17.0","8.18.0","8.20.0")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent

| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "jscrambler" and CommandLine has_any ("8.14.0","8.16.0","8.17.0","8.18.0","8.20.0")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Rust Infostealer Binary Execution from npm Post-Install Hook AIInstallation High
Detects the setup.js preinstall loader (run by node.exe/npm) writing a hidden, randomly-named native binary into the system temp directory and executing it detached. Matches on the three published payload hashes and on the node→temp-hidden-executable parent/child chain specific to this campaign. Rationale: Uses the three published decompressed payload SHA-256 values plus the article's described chain (setup.js under node writes a hidden .{random}/.{random}.exe into temp and launches it detached). Hash match is deterministic; the behavioral clause catches recompiled variants. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/jscrambler-supply-chain-attack • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-backdoor-jscrambler-npm-package-with-infostealer-malware/
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate node-gyp / native-addon builds that write and run compiled binaries from temp during install
  • Electron or Puppeteer post-install steps that unpack helper binaries into temp
  • Test frameworks that spawn short-lived helper executables from a temp workspace
  • A developer's own build tool that emits dot-prefixed cache files in temp
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("node-gyp","prebuild","electron-builder") and SHA256 !in~ ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd","b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903","c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: if a hash matches, this is confirmed malware — no further validation needed; for the behavioral hit, inspect the temp file name/signature and whether it was launched detached with hidden output. 2) Contain: isolate the host, terminate the temp process tree, and capture the binary for the DFIR queue before AV quarantine removes it. 3) Hunt: pivot on the process ID into UC3 (C2 to 37.27.122.124 / 57.128.246.79), UC4 (credential file access), and UC5 (persistence) on the same host and across all CI agents that pulled jscrambler in the July 11+ window.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where SHA256 in~ ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd","b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903","c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd")
   or (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe") and FolderPath has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\", "/tmp/", "/var/folders/") and FileName startswith ".")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SHA256 in~ ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd","b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903","c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd")
   or (ParentProcessName has_any ("node.exe","npm.exe") and ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (@"\Temp\", "/tmp/", "/var/folders/"))

IronWorm C2 beacon to hardcoded jscrambler stealer IPs AICommand & Control Medium
Detects any host reaching the two hard-coded attacker C2 IP addresses (37.27.122.124, 57.128.246.79) that StepSecurity observed the dropped jscrambler stealer contacting over TLS. Pure network-IOC pivot; independent of process telemetry so it catches the stealer even if EDR missed the drop. Rationale: Uses the two direct attacker C2 IPs StepSecurity published — the first network indicators for the campaign, confirmed across multiple write-ups. Static malicious IPs have essentially no legitimate business use. cloudwatch_query left empty: this is endpoint/firewall egress telemetry that does not live in CloudTrail, and VPC Flow fields fall outside the CloudTrail whitelist. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/jscrambler-supply-chain-attack • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-backdoor-jscrambler-npm-package-with-infostealer-malware/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A threat-intel enrichment or sandbox appliance deliberately connecting to the IOC IPs for analysis
  • A security researcher detonating the sample in a lab that shares the corporate egress
  • Shared cloud-provider IP reuse if the attacker infra is later reassigned (Hetzner/OVH ranges)
  • A vulnerability scanner probing the IPs as part of external attack-surface testing
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("sandbox","malware-lab","detonation"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process on the host — if it maps to a temp-dropped hidden binary or node.exe child, escalate to confirmed stealer C2. 2) Contain: block 37.27.122.124 and 57.128.246.79 at the perimeter/EDR, isolate the source host, and snapshot memory. 3) Hunt: sweep all egress logs for these IPs and Tor bootstrap traffic (check.torproject.org / archive.torproject.org) from build agents; correlate to UC1 installs and rotate every secret reachable from that host.

Credential/Browser Data Theft Post-npm Install AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects a hidden temp-directory process (the dropped Rust stealer) touching the specific secret stores the article enumerates: AWS/Azure/GCP credentials, .ssh keys, Chrome/Edge user data, Bitwarden/MetaMask/Exodus/Phantom wallets, and AI-coding-tool configs (Claude Desktop, Cursor, Windsurf, VS Code, Zed) that hold API keys and MCP credentials. Rationale: Pairs the article's exact target list (AWS/Azure/GCP, .ssh, Chrome/Edge, Bitwarden, MetaMask/Exodus/Phantom, and the newer AI-tool configs for Claude/Cursor/Windsurf/VS Code/Zed) with the initiating process being the hidden temp-dropped binary — the two together are far more specific than any single credential-store access. datadog_query empty: Sysmon does not emit reliable file-read events (EID 11 is create-only), so this read-centric detection cannot be faithfully expressed on Datadog Windows telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/jscrambler-supply-chain-attack

1) Triage: confirm the acting process is the hidden temp binary (dot-prefixed, random name) and not a signed vendor updater; check how many distinct secret stores it touched in the window. 2) Contain: isolate the host and preserve the binary; assume every accessed store is compromised. 3) Hunt: rotate the specific secrets touched — cloud keys, SSH keys, browser sessions, Bitwarden vault, and AI-tool/MCP API keys — then sweep other hosts that installed jscrambler for the same acting-process pattern.

Persistence written by temp-dropped binary (hidden sched task / macOS LaunchAgent) AIInstallation Medium
Detects the stealer wiring in reboot persistence: a hidden Windows scheduled task set to relaunch every minute (schtasks /create ... minute) spawned from a temp-directory process, or a macOS LaunchAgent plist written into ~/Library/LaunchAgents by a process running from /tmp or /var/folders. Rationale: Anchors on the article's precise persistence detail — a hidden scheduled task set to relaunch every minute, and a macOS LaunchAgent reloading on login — combined with the parent being the temp-dropped binary. The Sentinel query now keys on 4688 NewProcessName + CommandLine instead of the non-existent TaskName column. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-backdoor-jscrambler-npm-package-with-infostealer-malware/
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1543.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate software installers creating per-minute health-check tasks from a temp-extracted setup binary
  • Monitoring agents (RMM tools) registering frequent scheduled tasks during deployment
  • macOS app installers dropping a LaunchAgent plist from a staged installer in /var/folders
  • An admin script creating a recurring task while logged in from an elevated temp-run tool
Suppression filter
| where not (ParentProcessName has_any ("msiexec.exe","setup.exe") and CommandLine has_any ("Adobe","Google","Microsoft"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the task action/target binary (schtasks /query /tn <name> /xml) or the LaunchAgent plist contents — a target pointing to a hidden temp file is confirmed malicious. 2) Contain: delete the scheduled task / remove the LaunchAgent plist, kill the referenced binary, and isolate the host. 3) Hunt: search all jscrambler-affected hosts for per-minute tasks and unfamiliar ~/Library/LaunchAgents plists created since July 11, and correlate the task target hash against the UC2 payload hashes.
union
 (DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/create" and ProcessCommandLine has "minute" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\")
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Artifact = ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath),
 (DeviceFileEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where FolderPath has "/Library/LaunchAgents/" and FileName endswith ".plist" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("/tmp/","/var/folders/")
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName, Artifact = FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath)
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "schtasks.exe"
| where CommandLine has "/create" and CommandLine has "minute"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

jscrambler Package Tampering Artifact Detection AIDelivery Medium
Detects the tell-tale supply-chain artifacts of the compromise: the added dist/setup.js loader and dist/intro.js (a ~7.8MB binary container despite the .js name) appearing under node_modules/jscrambler, matched by the two published file hashes or by path+filename. These files exist in the npm tarball but nowhere in jscrambler's public source. Rationale: Uses the two published SHA-256 hashes for dist/setup.js and dist/intro.js plus the exact path/filename pattern (node_modules/jscrambler/dist). Multiple analysts (StepSecurity, SafeDep, Socket) confirmed these files exist in the tarball but not in the public repo, making their presence on disk high-fidelity supply-chain evidence. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/jscrambler-supply-chain-attack • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-backdoor-jscrambler-npm-package-with-infostealer-malware/
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An unrelated package or project that legitimately ships files named setup.js/intro.js in a directory containing 'jscrambler' in its path
  • A security researcher storing the extracted malicious files in a case folder path containing 'jscrambler'
  • A backup/restore operation replaying the tarball into a quarantined node_modules for analysis
  • A vendored copy of a clean older jscrambler release that happens to include a setup.js
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has_any ("\\case\\", "\\quarantine\\", "\\samples\\", "/analysis/"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash the on-disk setup.js/intro.js and compare to the published values; a match plus a ~7.8MB intro.js confirms the tampered package. 2) Contain: remove the node_modules/jscrambler tree and the lockfile pin, isolate the host if the preinstall hook already ran, and rebuild from a clean 8.13.0/8.15.0. 3) Hunt: search artifact registries, container images, and CI caches for these two hashes, then pivot to UC2/UC3 on any host where the files were present to confirm whether the payload executed.

| where SHA256 in~ ("a742de963f14a92d24ebcbc7b44ac867e23a20d31d1b0094a13a4f83287f4e60","a41a523ef9517aab37ed6eea0ec881821bdcb7aefcb5c5f603adc7907f868c86")
   or (FolderPath has "jscrambler" and FileName in~ ("setup.js","intro.js"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ActionType

   or (TargetFilePath has "jscrambler" and TargetFileName in~ ("setup.js","intro.js"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

    - attack.t1555.003

    product: windows

    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'

    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("a742de963f14a92d24ebcbc7b44ac867e23a20d31d1b0094a13a4f83287f4e60", "a41a523ef9517aab37ed6eea0ec881821bdcb7aefcb5c5f603adc7907f868c86", "fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd") or SHA1 in~ ("a742de963f14a92d24ebcbc7b44ac867e23a20d31d1b0094a13a4f83287f4e60", "a41a523ef9517aab37ed6eea0ec881821bdcb7aefcb5c5f603adc7907f868c86", "fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd") or MD5 in~ ("a742de963f14a92d24ebcbc7b44ac867e23a20d31d1b0094a13a4f83287f4e60", "a41a523ef9517aab37ed6eea0ec881821bdcb7aefcb5c5f603adc7907f868c86", "fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("a742de963f14a92d24ebcbc7b44ac867e23a20d31d1b0094a13a4f83287f4e60", "a41a523ef9517aab37ed6eea0ec881821bdcb7aefcb5c5f603adc7907f868c86", "fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd") or SHA1 in~ ("a742de963f14a92d24ebcbc7b44ac867e23a20d31d1b0094a13a4f83287f4e60", "a41a523ef9517aab37ed6eea0ec881821bdcb7aefcb5c5f603adc7907f868c86", "fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd") or MD5 in~ ("a742de963f14a92d24ebcbc7b44ac867e23a20d31d1b0094a13a4f83287f4e60", "a41a523ef9517aab37ed6eea0ec881821bdcb7aefcb5c5f603adc7907f868c86", "fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["a742de963f14a92d24ebcbc7b44ac867e23a20d31d1b0094a13a4f83287f4e60", "a41a523ef9517aab37ed6eea0ec881821bdcb7aefcb5c5f603adc7907f868c86", "fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

cms_plugin.exe Rust stager execution + payload pull from 193.42.25.65 AIInstallation High
Hunts the custom 'cms_plugin.exe' implant that masqueraded as a Complaint Management System portal update on Balochistan Police infrastructure. The Rust stager variant downloads a next stage from 193.42.25.65 and prints 'Update Complete! Please refresh the page'. Fires on the named binary executing or any host reaching the stager download IP. Rationale: cms_plugin.exe is a unique implant filename and 193.42.25.65 is the confirmed Rust-stager download server named in the SentinelLABS report; both are non-generic, so a match is effectively a true positive. Cross-checked SentinelOne report and The Record write-up. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/labs/one-target-china-india-espionage-converge-on-pakistani-law-enforcement/ • https://therecord.media/china-india-ran-separate-spy-campaigns-against-same-police-force
ATT&CKT1105 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimately-named plugin binary in an unrelated product also called cms_plugin.exe (rare; validate hash and path)
  • Security researcher / IR analyst detonating the sample in a sandbox VM enrolled in EDR
  • Threat-intel enrichment appliance actively probing 193.42.25.65 for research
  • Proxy/NAT egress IP collision where 193.42.25.65 is re-used by a benign CDN in future (validate at trigger time)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Sandbox\\" and DeviceName !in~ ("IR-SANDBOX-01")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the process tree, SHA256, and folder path for cms_plugin.exe; confirm parent (likely w3wp.exe/web-app service on a CMS/web server) and whether the host is an internet-facing police web application server. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block 193.42.25.65 at the perimeter, and preserve the binary for reversing. 3) Hunt: sweep all web servers for cms_plugin.exe uploads, search web logs on cms.balochistanpolice.gov.pk-style portals for the file, and pivot on the SHA1s and the full campaign C2 IP set (see C2 UC).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "193.42.25.65" or InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "cms_plugin.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
union
(SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where tolower(NewProcessName) endswith "\\cms_plugin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, Signal="process", NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, Dest=""),
(CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP == "193.42.25.65"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer=SourceHostName, Account=SourceUserName, Signal="network", NewProcessName=ProcessName, CommandLine="", ParentProcessName="", Dest=DestinationIP)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Fake 360Safe.exe (.NET) reflectively loading AsyncRAT AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the second cms_plugin.exe variant: a .NET executable that masquerades as '360Safe.exe' (a legitimate Qihoo 360 Total Security binary) to reflectively load an in-memory AsyncRAT client. Detects a process named 360Safe.exe whose file metadata is NOT Qihoo/360 or which runs from outside the legitimate 360 install path. Rationale: The report states one implant variant masquerades specifically as 360Safe.exe (Qihoo 360) to reflectively load AsyncRAT; a 360Safe.exe binary running outside the genuine Qihoo install path (or lacking Qihoo file metadata) is a high-fidelity masquerade signal, especially in a Pakistani gov environment unlikely to run Chinese AV. Corroborated by SentinelOne report and Kaspersky's Mysterious Elephant AsyncRAT/Remcos tradecraft. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/labs/one-target-china-india-espionage-converge-on-pakistani-law-enforcement/ • https://securelist.com/mysterious-elephant-apt-ttps-and-tools/117596/
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1620
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine Qihoo 360 Total Security installed to a non-default drive/path (validate publisher signature)
  • Portable/standalone 360 Total Security run from a USB or Downloads folder by a user
  • Software-deployment tool staging the real 360Safe.exe in a temp cache before install
  • AV bake-off / procurement testing of 360 Total Security by IT
Suppression filter
| where not(ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has_any ("360","Qihoo"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: check the digital signature and ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName of the 360Safe.exe image — genuine is signed by Qihoo/360; the implant will be unsigned or mis-signed. Inspect for .NET/CLR module loads and outbound connections. 2) Contain: isolate the host, capture memory (AsyncRAT is in-memory), block associated C2 IPs. 3) Hunt: search DeviceImageLoadEvents for clr.dll/mscoree loading into 360Safe.exe, and correlate with cms_plugin.exe drops and the campaign C2 IP set.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "360Safe.exe"
| where not(ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has_any ("360","Qihoo")) or FolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName, ProcessVersionInfoProductName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where tolower(NewProcessName) endswith "\\360safe.exe"
| where not(tolower(NewProcessName) startswith "c:\\program files (x86)\\360\\") and not(tolower(NewProcessName) startswith "c:\\program files\\360\\")
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName

Beaconing to Balochistan Police espionage C2 / stager IP set AICommand & Control High
Hunts outbound connections to the confirmed command-and-control and staging IPs across the four converging clusters (Cobalt Strike C2 142.171.183.8, Rust-stager host 193.42.25.65, plus the campaign infrastructure block) targeting Pakistani law enforcement. Any internal host reaching these IPs warrants investigation. Rationale: 142.171.183.8 is the named Cobalt Strike C2 and 193.42.25.65 the stager host; the remaining IPs are the pre-extracted campaign infrastructure. These are static, second-source-consistent IOCs, so egress to any of them is high-fidelity for this specific converging-actor campaign. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/labs/one-target-china-india-espionage-converge-on-pakistani-law-enforcement/ • https://therecord.media/china-india-ran-separate-spy-campaigns-against-same-police-force
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An IOC IP later reassigned to a shared hosting/CDN provider serving benign sites (re-validate WHOIS at trigger time)
  • Internal threat-intel platform or vulnerability scanner actively probing the C2 IPs
  • Security researcher pivoting on the infrastructure from a corporate egress IP
  • Firewall/proxy that logs a blocked (denied) attempt — confirm DeviceAction/outcome is allow before escalating
Suppression filter
DeviceNetworkEvents | where ActionType in ("ConnectionSuccess","ConnectionAttempt") and RemoteIPType == "Public"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the source host and the InitiatingProcess making the connection; check whether the connection succeeded vs was blocked, and beacon regularity (jitter/interval). 2) Contain: block all listed IPs at the perimeter, isolate any host with a successful/repeated connection, and snapshot memory for the process (PlugX/ShadowPad/Cobalt Strike/AsyncRAT are memory-resident). 3) Hunt: pivot on the initiating process hash against the campaign SHA1 list, sweep for cms_plugin.exe and fake 360Safe.exe, and review the FortiMail email gateway and web-app servers for the initial foothold.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("142.171.183.8","193.42.25.65","41.216.188.140","89.31.121.220","45.125.32.218","172.111.233.36","172.111.233.96","172.111.233.12","172.111.233.105","172.111.233.26","172.94.9.49","172.94.9.43","172.94.9.19","45.74.6.17")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Conns=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort,10) by DeviceName, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by LastSeen desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP in ("142.171.183.8","193.42.25.65","41.216.188.140","89.31.121.220","45.125.32.218","172.111.233.36","172.111.233.96","172.111.233.12","172.111.233.105","172.111.233.26","172.94.9.49","172.94.9.43","172.94.9.19","45.74.6.17")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Conns=count(), Ports=make_set(DestinationPort,10) by SourceIP, SourceHostName, DestinationIP, DeviceProduct
| order by LastSeen desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("142.171.183.8", "193.42.25.65", "41.216.188.140", "89.31.121.220", "45.125.32.218", "172.111.233.36", "172.111.233.96", "172.111.233.12", "172.111.233.105", "172.111.233.26", "172.94.9.49", "172.94.9.43", "172.94.9.19", "45.74.6.17") or RemoteUrl has_any ("cms.balochistanpolice.gov.pk")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
let BadIPs     = dynamic(["142.171.183.8", "193.42.25.65", "41.216.188.140", "89.31.121.220", "45.125.32.218", "172.111.233.36", "172.111.233.96", "172.111.233.12", "172.111.233.105", "172.111.233.26", "172.94.9.49", "172.94.9.43", "172.94.9.19", "45.74.6.17"]);
let BadDomains = dynamic(["cms.balochistanpolice.gov.pk"]);
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr in (BadIPs)
   or Url has_any (BadDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Outbound Connection to Article-Named IP / Domain
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0f
status: experimental
description: |
    Replace `__IP_LIST__` / `__DOMAIN_LIST__` placeholders with
    article-specific destinations. For dynamic IOC management, use a
    watchlist or external feed.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0011/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.command-and-control
logsource:
    category: network_connection
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_ip:
        DestinationIp:
            - '__IP_PLACEHOLDER_1__'
            - '__IP_PLACEHOLDER_2__'
    selection_domain:
        DestinationHostname:
            - '__DOMAIN_PLACEHOLDER_1__'
            - '__DOMAIN_PLACEHOLDER_2__'
    condition: selection_ip or selection_domain
falsepositives:
    - None on a true-positive IOC match
level: critical

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["23f6781919a50b118d8d4e6a7e9ae63b71ecc885", "4039454c9189e64285e93fc075a30b93f814b5b5", "58cb2d95063b9df807b7aa8dc106b74ce988a491", "000fad96a85dd6933c22d3dbec9aed47b7f1f066", "08570471f39bb6725f07b8cddbea99ed48c22686", "23f4766c011d193f076dfc735dc460e2a41ead79", "47f8cb0c2dcf62702f58cfc1603d6325755f6820", "5d60ff36ff519c2e13e7f66cfa0bb46be79592a7", "63b88d00331de88af696dfb7a896935d830e485f", "8c329db96e093fa25268e078405a33c518dbb5c9", "d66ab0cd2e44dc8389c111b7ea34c7bcb0b35311", "2bab40c55637398f0497cff9c8cbea564d595c7f", "539bd79fbb684edea94eb37518134b97e94b9dd8", "6fe2e74d009abbd56de01fd7404a1245e9b47c79", "71757adba833b46f961e840d0f055bcce0b529c4", "c6c197e61079a0a33108c2c87b5e3c7056a138ec"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: File or Process Matching Article Hash IOCs
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0b
status: experimental
description: |
    Replace `__HASH_LIST__` placeholder with article-specific SHA256
    values. Use a watchlist or external indicator file for management
    at scale.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        Hashes|contains:
            - 'SHA256=__HASH_PLACEHOLDER_REPLACE_ME__'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - None on a true-positive hash match
level: critical

Critical Zimbra Flaw Could Let Crafted Emails Run Malicious Code in User Sessions

The Hacker News
2026-07-11 11 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Zimbra is urging customers to apply updates to address a critical security vulnerability impacting the Classic Web Client that could result in arbitrary code execution. The vulnerability has been described as a case of stored cross-site scripting (XSS) that could allow specially crafted emails to execute malicious scripts in a user's session. It has yet to be assigned a CVE identifier. "The

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Zimbra crafted-email XSS payload: HTML event-handler / <details ontoggle> in mail or SOAP traffic
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Vulnerable Zimbra Classic Web Client exposure (ZCS < 10.1.19)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Zimbra malicious sieve filter creating external mail-forwarding rule (post-XSS takeover) · [LLM] Zimbra webmail session mass mailbox harvest via SOAP (bulk Search/GetMsg) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Vulnerable Zimbra Classic Web Client exposure (ZCS < 10.1.19) AIExploitation High
Surfaces Zimbra Collaboration Suite hosts running a Classic Web Client build below the patched 10.1.19 release, which are exposed to the Google TAG-reported stored-XSS RCE and the closely-related exploited CVE-2025-27915. Pure exposure/attack-surface hunt keyed on the exact fixed version the vendor published. Rationale: Uses the exact vendor-published patched build (ZCS 10.1.19) from the Zimbra advisory / BleepingComputer / SecurityWeek to compute a precise sub-version exposure list; anything <10.1.19 on the 10.1 line, plus all 9.x/10.0.x, runs the vulnerable Classic Web Client. Corroborated the fixed version and Google TAG attribution across three independent write-ups. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/zimbra-urges-customers-to-patch-critical-web-client-xss-flaw/ • https://www.securityweek.com/zimbra-patches-critical-code-execution-vulnerability/ • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-27915
ATT&CKT1203
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Zimbra host mid-upgrade where inventory hasn't re-scanned to reflect 10.1.19
  • Zimbra deployments using only the Modern UI (not exploitable) but still flagged on version
  • Network appliance bundling an old embedded Zimbra library reported by the scanner
  • Dev/test Zimbra instance intentionally pinned to an old build
  • TVM version string with non-numeric patch suffix (e.g. 10.1.5_GA) parsed leniently
Suppression filter
| where EndOfSupportStatus != "Upgrade required" or isnotempty(SoftwareVersion)
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the host actually serves the Classic Web Client (/zimbra vs /modern) and the build is truly <10.1.19; cross-check against change tickets for an in-progress patch. Step 2 (contain): Prioritise internet-facing Zimbra for immediate upgrade to 10.1.19; where patching lags, disable the Classic Web Client / restrict access to the mail UI. Step 3 (hunt): For any exposed host, run UC-A and UC-D against its mailbox/audit logs for the last 30 days to rule out prior exploitation (rogue forwarding filters, SOAP harvest bursts).
DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
| where SoftwareVendor has "zimbra" or SoftwareName has "zimbra"
| extend v = split(SoftwareVersion, ".")
| extend vMajor = toint(v[0]), vMinor = toint(v[1]), vPatch = toint(extract(@"^(\d+)", 1, tostring(v[2])))
| where isnotempty(vMajor)
| where vMajor < 10 or (vMajor == 10 and vMinor < 1) or (vMajor == 10 and vMinor == 1 and vPatch < 19)
| project DeviceId, DeviceName, OSPlatform, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, EndOfSupportStatus
| sort by SoftwareVersion asc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where SoftwareVendor has "zimbra" or SoftwareName has "zimbra"
| extend v = split(SoftwareVersion, ".")
| extend vMajor = toint(v[0]), vMinor = toint(v[1]), vPatch = toint(extract(@"^(\d+)", 1, tostring(v[2])))
| where isnotempty(vMajor)
| where vMajor < 10 or (vMajor == 10 and vMinor < 1) or (vMajor == 10 and vMinor == 1 and vPatch < 19)
| summarize CveIds = make_set(CveId, 20), MaxSeverity = max(VulnerabilitySeverityLevel) by DeviceName, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, bin(TimeGenerated, 1d)
| sort by SoftwareVersion asc

Zimbra crafted-email XSS payload: HTML event-handler / <details ontoggle> in mail or SOAP traffic AIDelivery Medium
Detects the delivery of the crafted-email XSS payload against Zimbra Classic Web Client by matching HTML5 event-handler injection (ontoggle, onerror, onload) and script/javascript: sink strings in inbound mail, ICS calendar content, or Zimbra web (SOAP/REST) traffic. Modeled directly on the CVE-2025-27915 in-the-wild payload that used a <details ontoggle=> handler inside an ICS attachment. Rationale: Payload strings (ontoggle / <details / onerror / javascript:) are taken from the confirmed CVE-2025-27915 in-the-wild ICS payload that abused the same Classic Web Client renderer this new flaw lives in; scoping to Zimbra /service/soap and /h/ endpoints keeps it specific to the mail app rather than generic web XSS. Defender left empty because Zimbra inbound mail/ICS content is not present in Advanced Hunting tables unless relayed through M365. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2025-27915/ • https://thehackernews.com/2025/10/zimbra-zero-day-exploited-to-target.html
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1203
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Marketing/newsletter HTML mail legitimately containing onload/onerror image handlers
  • Security-team phishing simulations carrying benign script markers
  • WAF pen-test or vulnerability scan probing the Zimbra web UI with XSS strings
  • Developers pasting HTML snippets into calendar/notes bodies
  • URL-encoded '<script' in a legitimate query parameter unrelated to exploitation
Suppression filter
| where RequestURL has_any ("/service/soap","/h/") and Message has "<details"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the full request/message; confirm the event handler sits in attacker-controlled mail/ICS content (not a template) and identify the recipient mailbox and Zimbra build (cross-ref UC-C). Step 2 (contain): Quarantine the message across all mailboxes by content hash, block the sender, and force-logout/reset the affected recipient's Zimbra session. Step 3 (hunt): Run UC-A (rogue forwarding filter) and UC-D (SOAP harvest) for the recipient over the following 72h — the CVE-2025-27915 payload fired on a 60s delay and re-harvested every 3 days, so check a multi-day window.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DestinationServiceName has "zimbra" or RequestURL has "/service/soap" or RequestURL has "/h/" or DeviceVendor has_any ("Zimbra","ModSecurity","Imperva","Barracuda","Fortinet")
| where Message has_any ("ontoggle","onerror=","onload=","onmouseover=","onanimationstart","<details","javascript:","<script")
   or RequestURL has_any ("ontoggle","%3Cdetails","%3Cscript","javascript%3A")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationServiceName, RequestMethod, RequestURL, Message
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Zimbra malicious sieve filter creating external mail-forwarding rule (post-XSS takeover) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects creation/modification of a Zimbra mailbox filter (sieve) that redirects incoming mail to an external/personal webmail address — the exact post-exploitation action of the Zimbra Classic Web Client XSS chain, which programmatically added a filter named 'Correo' forwarding to spam_to_junk@proton.me. High-fidelity account-takeover / exfil signal. Rationale: Uses the concrete, cross-source-confirmed post-exploitation IOCs from the exploited Zimbra Classic Web Client XSS: filter name 'Correo', target spam_to_junk@proton.me, plus a generalized sieve actionRedirect-to-external-webmail heuristic so it also catches variant forwarding addresses. Zimbra sieve/filter changes are not represented in Defender AH, so defender_kql is intentionally empty. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2025/10/zimbra-zero-day-exploited-to-target.html • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2025-27915/ • https://securityaffairs.com/183014/hacking/zimbra-users-targeted-in-zero-day-exploit-using-icalendar-attachments.html
ATT&CKT1114.003 T1564.008
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User legitimately configuring auto-forward of their own mail to a personal Gmail/Proton account
  • Admin-created org-wide journaling/archival filter to an external partner
  • Migration tooling that recreates forwarding rules in bulk
  • Helpdesk configuring a delegate/forward for a departing employee
  • Legitimate mailing-list plumbing using redirect actions
Suppression filter
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("Correo","spam_to_junk","proton.me") or (SyslogMessage has "actionRedirect" and not(SyslogMessage has "@yourorg"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Retrieve the full sieve script and the account+client IP (oip) that created it; confirm the user did not knowingly set up forwarding and check whether the client IP matches their normal geo/device. Step 2 (contain): Delete the rogue filter, reset the account password and revoke active Zimbra sessions/tokens, and block outbound forwarding to the target address at the gateway. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the creating client IP/session to enumerate other mailboxes it touched; run UC-D for that account to gauge how much mail was already harvested, and UC-B for the delivering crafted email.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("ModifyFilterRulesRequest","CreateFilterRulesRequest","zimbraMailSieveScript","actionRedirect")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("Correo","spam_to_junk","proton.me","protonmail.com")
   or (SyslogMessage has "actionRedirect" and SyslogMessage matches regex @"(?i)actionRedirect[^\n]{0,120}@(gmail|outlook|yandex|mail\.ru|proton(mail)?\.(me|com))")
| extend Account = extract(@"name=([^;]+);", 1, SyslogMessage)
| extend ClientIp = extract(@"oip=([0-9\.]+)", 1, SyslogMessage)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostName, ProcessName, Account, ClientIp, SyslogMessage
| sort by TimeGenerated desc
